title: Everything Is a Rollout — Alex Shaw + Ryan Marten, Terminal-Bench, Harbor, Laude Institute
talk_summary: Alex Shaw and Ryan Marten present Harbor, an open-source framework and directory format for specifying agentic environments (instruction + sandbox + verifier) and running rollouts in parallel across any agent, model, sandbox, and task. They argue agent development is more like ML than software engineering, so agent performance should be treated as a black box managed by empirical evaluation, and they show use cases including internal-codebase evals, prod rollouts, and map-reduce over trajectories.

takeaways.technique: Build an internal eval set from your own codebase/tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: They describe teams building private benchmarks from their own internal codebases (e.g. Ramp's RampBench) so model/agent choices are made on their real use cases rather than public benchmarks or brand trust.
takeaways.evidence_quote: start with the aval that matters and your ability to grade the outcome and then say I welcome all models

takeaways.what_they_do: Harbor defines a portable directory layout (instruction, sandbox, verifier) and runs rollouts in parallel across any sandbox, so tasks are interoperable and throughput scales by parallelism.
takeaways.evidence_quote: an open-source framework for performing rollouts in parallel using any agent with any model in any sandbox on any task
takeaways.numbers: example: 64 in parallel; launch mode for 10,000 rollouts overnight

takeaways.technique: Map-reduce over agent trajectories to find recurring mistakes
takeaways.what_they_do: They run a cheap fast model (Cursor CLI) over many past sessions to extract mistake/reason/correction JSON, then a stronger model reduces to a summary of recurring failure categories, which feeds new eval tasks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: summarize recurring mistakes and failure categories into a concise feedback.mmd file
takeaways.numbers: demo limited to 32 sessions; they note 1,000-10,000 is feasible

takeaways.technique: Prod rollouts / agentic map-reduce as a workload pattern
takeaways.what_they_do: Beyond evals, they run many agents in parallel sandboxes on production tasks (processing receipts, searching notes, asking questions over many PRs) and aggregate results intelligently.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you just want to run a ton of agents on distributed compute. of sandboxes in parallel and then somehow aggregate those results

takeaways.technique: Cheap model for map, strong model for reduce
takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately use a cheap fast CLI model for the high-volume map step and a stronger model only for the single reduce/summarization step where accuracy matters.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I do the map step with cursor CLI because it's cheap and fast. And then I do the reduce step with fable 5 because I wanted to have like an accurate summary

takeaways.technique: Verifier as programmatic reward per task
takeaways.what_they_do: Each environment pairs the agent run with a verifier (programmatic tests or rubric) that produces a reward, aggregated across rollouts into a pass rate.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need some way of telling whether or not the agent actually did the thing that we told it to do
